segments.voice: Yesterday in the Devi Mahatmya, the gods asked why the goddess didn't simply burn Mahisha with a look, and she left them a promise: remember me in trouble, and I will come. Who got your small good wish? Day one thousand sixty-seven.
screen: `THE DEVI MAHATMYA.` · `REMEMBER ME, AND I WILL COME.`

segments.voice: To the goddess who lives in all beings as consciousness: bow to her, bow to her, bow to her, again and again. That's the shape of a refrain the gods sing in the fifth chapter, over and over, changing one word each time. The third story has begun. Two demon brothers, Shumbha and Nishumbha, have taken over heaven, seized the sun's work and the moon's and the wind's, and thrown the gods out. And the gods do what they promised to do. They remember the goddess. They go to the Himalaya, and they start to sing. Today, the refrain, and the first move the demons make.
screen: `TWO DEMON BROTHERS TAKE HEAVEN.` → `THE GODS REMEMBER HER.` → `THEY START TO SING.`

segments.voice: Listen to what changes in the refrain. In paraphrase: the goddess who lives in all beings as consciousness. As understanding. As sleep. As hunger. As shadow. As power. As thirst. As patience. As modesty. As peace. As faith. As loveliness. As good fortune. As memory. As compassion. As contentment. As mother. And, near the end, as error. Each time: bow to her, bow to her, bow to her, again and again. Look at that list. It isn't only the noble things. Hunger is there. Sleep is there. Thirst. Even error is named. In this hymn the goddess isn't up on a mountain away from ordinary life. She's in the ordinary states a living being passes through in a day. Then the story moves. Parvati, Shiva's wife, comes down to bathe in the Ganges and asks: who are you praising? And from her own body a goddess steps out and answers for them: this hymn is for me. Two of Shumbha's servants, Chanda and Munda, see her on the mountain and run to their master. They describe a woman so beautiful that a king who owns every treasure ought to have her too. So Shumbha sends a messenger with a proposal: marry me, or my brother. The goddess smiles. In paraphrase, she says: what you say is true. But long ago, without much thought, I made a vow. Only the one who defeats me in battle, who takes away my pride, who is my equal in strength, can be my husband. So let him come and win me. The messenger warns her she's being foolish. She doesn't move.
screen: `IN ALL BEINGS AS CONSCIOUSNESS.` · `AS HUNGER, AS SLEEP, AS ERROR.` · `A GODDESS STEPS OUT OF PARVATI.` · `ONLY ONE WHO DEFEATS ME.` · then, large: `BOW TO HER, AGAIN AND AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let the refrain walk through you. Settle, and breathe. Then, without forcing anything, notice what's here, one state at a time, the way the hymn lists them. Is there hunger? Notice it. Tiredness? Notice it. Some patience, some restlessness, a memory? Notice each one, and let each have a breath. Don't sort them into good and bad. The hymn didn't. If you pray, you can bow inwardly to the goddess at each one, as the gods do. If you don't, simply let each be seen. The bell holds the time.
The Devi Mahatmya. Today, the third story's opening: a refrain to the goddess who lives in all beings, even as hunger and error, and her vow to Shumbha.
Your line: the Devi Mahatmya, read whole. Today, when you're hungry or tired or wrong, notice it once without scolding, as one more thing the hymn makes room for. Day one thousand sixty-seven.

howItsDone: The refrain of the fifth chapter, beginning 'ya devi sarvabhuteshu', is also chanted on its own by some Hindus, at home and in temples, including during Navaratri.

original.note: Sanskrit: yā devī sarvabhūteṣu, 'the goddess who in all beings…', the opening of each line of the refrain.

trapdoor: what you thought: a goddess praised for being powerful and pure.
what it means: the gods bow to her as every state of a living being, hunger and sleep and error included; then she meets Shumbha's proposal with a vow.
what a scholar hears: chapter 5, the hymn sometimes called the Aparajita Stuti, with its repeated namas tasyai, namas tasyai, namas tasyai namo namaḥ.

notes: Chapter 5 paraphrased. Refrain list (yā devī sarvabhūteṣu … rūpeṇa saṃsthitā): cetanā (consciousness), buddhi, nidrā, kṣudhā, chāyā, śakti, tṛṣṇā, kṣānti, lajjā, śānti, śraddhā, kānti, lakṣmī, smṛti, dayā, tuṣṭi, mātṛ, bhrānti. The script lists them in roughly this order but skips some (e.g. jāti, vṛtti) and the opening Vishnumaya line; confirm order and renderings ('error' for bhrānti, 'loveliness' for kānti).
The hook renders the refrain's shape ('bow to her, bow to her, bow to her, again and again') as a paraphrase; it is not quoted from any translation.

Ambika/Kaushiki emerges from Parvati's body (kośa) and says the hymn is addressed to her; Parvati then becomes dark (Kalika). The script names only 'a goddess steps out'; tomorrow's Kali is a separate emergence from Ambika's brow. Confirm.
Shumbha's offer: the goddess may marry him or Nishumbha. Her vow: whoever conquers her in battle, removes her pride and is her equal in strength. 'Without much thought' renders alpabuddhi; confirm.
howItsDone says the refrain is also chanted on its own, including during Navaratri; confirm.
Editor pass: trapdoor 'often called the Aparajita Stuti' softened to 'sometimes'; howItsDone now says 'some Hindus' rather than implying general practice.
